title: Inverted Right Half Pyramid
description: Brute force to optimized: per-character printing versus building each shrinking row directly by its known length, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, print a right angled triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains n minus i plus 1 stars, shrinking by one star every row.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a right angled triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains n minus i plus 1 stars, left aligned, so the pattern starts wide and shrinks by one star on every following row.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Pyramid Turned Upside Down
blocks.text: This is the same growing triangle seen earlier, just flipped from top to bottom. Instead of starting with one star and growing wider, it starts as wide as possible and loses exactly one star on every row that follows, until only a single star remains on the very last row.

blocks.caption: Row i always holds n minus i plus 1 stars, shrinking down toward 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","****","Row 1 has n minus i plus 1, which is 4, the widest row in the whole pattern."],["Row 2","***","One fewer star than the row above, following the shrinking formula."],["Row 3","**","Continuing to shrink by one star per row."],["Row 4","*","The final, narrowest row, exactly 1 star as the formula guarantees."]]}

blocks.text: No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what genuinely changes when a familiar pattern gets flipped.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This shape is the exact same triangle as before, just flipped top to bottom, so instead of growing by one star per row it shrinks by one star per row.

Observation 2: Despite shrinking instead of growing, row i's exact length is still fully known in advance, simply n minus i plus 1 instead of i.

Observation 3: Since only the length formula changed, not the underlying technique, the same direct-construction idea, build a row of known length in one operation, applies without any further changes.

Observation 4: And since every row's construction is still independent of the others, all n rows can still be built first and joined into a single output call, exactly as with the growing version.
That reasoning alone already tells us this is not a new problem, just a new formula plugged into the same known technique.
Use an outer loop for each row i from 1 to n, and an inner loop that runs exactly n minus i plus 1 times, printing a single star character on every iteration.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Compute how many stars this row needs, n minus i plus 1.
Print a single star for each of those, one print call per character.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: print one star at a time, one call per character

codes.python:
def inverted_right_half_pyramid(n):
    for i in range(1, n + 1):                  # row i needs n - i + 1 stars
        stars = n - i + 1
        for j in range(stars):                  # print each star in this row
            print("*", end="")                    # one call per character
        print()                                 # move to the next line after the row


if __name__ == "__main__":
    inverted_right_half_pyramid(4)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: stars is computed once per row, using the shrinking formula n minus i plus 1, before the inner loop even begins, so the inner loop's bound is set once rather than recomputed on every character.
A single star is printed per innermost iteration, the smallest possible unit of output, keeping the true per-character cost of this version fully visible.
The line break happens once per outer iteration, exactly mirroring the growing version's structure, only the row-length formula itself has changed.

blocks.text: This is correct, since row i always ends up with exactly n minus i plus 1 stars printed, one at a time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total stars across all rows is n plus n minus 1 plus down to 1, proportional to n squared, and each star costs its own print call.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: printing one character at a time means as many output calls as there are stars. Since the exact length of each row is already known in advance, that entire row can be built in a single operation instead, needing only one print call per row rather than one per character.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why printing one star at a time works but is wasteful: it is the same roughly n squared over 2 total output calls as the growing version, just shrinking instead of growing.

What stays the same as the growing pyramid: the underlying insight, row length is known before the row starts, so it can be built directly.

What actually changes here: only the formula for that known length, n minus i plus 1 instead of i.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a repeat operation still builds the row in one step, regardless of which formula computed the length.

The core idea: build each row directly at its shrinking length, n minus i plus 1, then print it once.

For each row i, build a string of exactly n minus i plus 1 stars in one operation, using a direct repeat rather than appending characters one by one, then print that row with a single call. This cuts the number of print calls from roughly n squared down to just n, one per row.
For each row i, build the row directly at its shrinking length, n minus i plus 1, then print it once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build each shrinking row directly, one print call per row

blocks.text: This works because row i's length, n minus i plus 1, is just as fully known ahead of time as it was in the growing version, only the formula itself has reversed direction; a direct repeat operation still constructs exactly that many stars in one step, with no dependence on any other row's contents. As i increases from 1 to n, n minus i plus 1 decreases from n down to 1, producing the correct shrinking sequence of row lengths.

items: The row length is computed as n minus i plus 1 directly inside the outer loop, immediately reversing the growing formula from the earlier pyramid problem into a shrinking one.
A direct repeat operation constructs the entire row using that computed length in one step, exactly the same construction technique as the growing version, just fed a different number.
Each row is printed immediately after being built, one output call per row, with the natural shrinkage handled entirely by the length formula, not by any special casing in the loop itself.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, since that is the size of the output, but only O(n) print calls are made instead of O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly at its own shrinking length, n minus i plus 1, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is deferring output until every row exists.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete shrinking pattern as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole triangle, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: Flipping a familiar pattern upside down is usually just a matter of reversing the formula that determines row length, from growing by 1 each row to shrinking by 1 each row. The same output batching ideas, building a full row in one operation and then the full pattern in one call, apply just as well here as they did for the growing version.

items: Using the wrong formula for row length, n minus i instead of n minus i plus 1, which shifts every row off by one star.
Forgetting that the very last row still needs exactly 1 star, not 0.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: Recognizing that this pattern is simply the mirror image, top to bottom, of an earlier one is a useful shortcut, it means the same row building and output batching approach can be reused directly, with only the length formula needing to change.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this different from the growing pyramid", think: only the length formula reverses direction, n minus i plus 1 instead of i, the underlying technique is identical.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid growing the row one character at a time", think: build each row directly at its known, shrinking length.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is the number of output operations: roughly O(n squared) individual calls in the brute force version, O(n) calls in the optimized version, and exactly one call in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing where each row's length is known in advance via a shrinking formula, the mirror image of a growing pyramid, built directly instead of character by character.

Core Idea: row i always needs exactly n minus i plus 1 stars, a length known before that row is built and reached by simply reversing the growing formula, so a direct repeat operation constructs it in one step, and joining every row allows a single output call.
Time: O(n squared) output calls for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: reversing a familiar pattern's direction is usually just a formula change, not a new algorithm.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shrinking shape; recognizing it as the same technique as the growing version, just mirrored, is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: same known-length direct construction as the growing pyramid, just with n minus i plus 1 instead of i.
